name: Small solid kick motor (Star 37 class)
tradeoff: The cheapest push there is: one fixed kick, direction only.
source: Star 37FM: 1147.4 kg loaded, 1065.9 kg propellant, 289.8 s, 47.26 kN. Northrop Grumman Propulsion Products Catalog, values as tabulated in Wikipedia, "Star (rocket stage)". Rounded. The cost is a game value, not a real price.

name: Solid motor (Star 48 class)
tradeoff: Cheap and simple, but fires once and burns everything.
source: Star 48B: 2133.7 kg loaded, 2011 kg propellant, 286 s, about 67 kN. Northrop Grumman Propulsion Products Catalog, values as tabulated in Wikipedia, "Star 48". Rounded. The cost is a game value, not a real price.

name: Large solid booster (Orion 50S XL class)
tradeoff: A whole first stage in one cheap part, but it cannot be throttled or stopped.
source: Orion 50S XL (Pegasus XL first stage): 16173 kg loaded, 1092 kg at burnout, 69.1 s burn; Wikipedia, "Orion (rocket stage)". The specific impulse (295 s) is an estimate for a motor of this class and the thrust is derived from it and the burn time. The cost is a game value, not a real price.

name: Cold-gas thruster
tradeoff: Tiny, cheap and restartable, but very wasteful with propellant.
source: Nitrogen cold gas: specific impulse 65 to 70 s, thrust 10 mN to 10 N; NASA State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology, in-space propulsion chapter. The mass is an estimate. The cost is a game value, not a real price.

name: Small upper-stage engine (Rutherford class)
tradeoff: Light and efficient for pulses in orbit; too weak to lift a big rocket off the pad.
source: Rutherford vacuum engine: 25.8 kN, 343 s, 35 kg; Rocket Lab, as listed in Wikipedia, "Rutherford (rocket engine)". The cost is a game value, not a real price.

name: Booster engine (Merlin class)
tradeoff: Strong enough to lift a heavy rocket and can fire several times, but needs a separate tank.
source: Merlin 1D: 845 kN at sea level, 311 s in vacuum (282 s at sea level), 470 kg; SpaceX, as listed in Wikipedia, "SpaceX Merlin". The game uses the vacuum specific impulse; the mission's launch loss covers the rest. The cost is a game value, not a real price.

name: Hydrogen upper-stage engine (RL10 class)
tradeoff: The most velocity change per kilogram of propellant, at the highest price.
source: RL10B-2: 110.1 kN, 465.5 s, 301 kg; Aerojet Rocketdyne, as listed in Wikipedia, "RL10". Rounded. The cost is a game value, not a real price.

name: Large aluminium tank
tradeoff: Cheap and heavy. Regulated pressure keeps every pulse at full strength.
source: Dry mass is 4.8% of the propellant capacity. Ratio of the Space Shuttle's first External Tank (aluminium 2219, about 35000 kg empty, 735601 kg of propellant); NASA figures as listed in Wikipedia, "Space Shuttle external tank". Scaled down from a 735-tonne tank, so a real tank this small would be somewhat heavier. The cost is a game value, not a real price.

name: Large aluminium-lithium tank
tradeoff: A quarter lighter than aluminium for the same propellant, at a higher price.
source: Dry mass is 3.6% of the propellant capacity. Ratio of the Space Shuttle Super Lightweight Tank (aluminium-lithium 2195, 26500 kg empty, 735601 kg of propellant); NASA fact sheet "Super Lightweight External Tank". Scaled down from a 735-tonne tank, so a real tank this small would be somewhat heavier. The cost is a game value, not a real price.

name: Large carbon-composite tank
tradeoff: The lightest large tank, and the most expensive.
source: Dry mass is 2.5% of the propellant capacity. The aluminium-lithium ratio less 30%, the weight-saving goal of NASA's Composite Cryotank Technologies and Demonstration project. Scaled down from a 735-tonne tank, so a real tank this small would be somewhat heavier. The cost is a game value, not a real price.

name: Small aluminium tank
tradeoff: A cheap upper-stage tank. Blowdown pressure falls as it empties.
source: Dry mass is 4.8% of the propellant capacity. Ratio of the Space Shuttle's first External Tank (aluminium 2219, about 35000 kg empty, 735601 kg of propellant); NASA figures as listed in Wikipedia, "Space Shuttle external tank". Scaled down from a 735-tonne tank, so a real tank this small would be somewhat heavier. The cost is a game value, not a real price.

name: Small aluminium-lithium tank
tradeoff: Lighter upper-stage tank. Blowdown pressure falls as it empties.
source: Dry mass is 3.6% of the propellant capacity. Ratio of the Space Shuttle Super Lightweight Tank (aluminium-lithium 2195, 26500 kg empty, 735601 kg of propellant); NASA fact sheet "Super Lightweight External Tank". Scaled down from a 735-tonne tank, so a real tank this small would be somewhat heavier. The cost is a game value, not a real price.

name: Small carbon-composite tank
tradeoff: The lightest upper-stage tank. Blowdown pressure falls as it empties.
source: Dry mass is 2.5% of the propellant capacity. The aluminium-lithium ratio less 30%, the weight-saving goal of NASA's Composite Cryotank Technologies and Demonstration project. Scaled down from a 735-tonne tank, so a real tank this small would be somewhat heavier. The cost is a game value, not a real price.

name: Basic altimeter
tradeoff: Shows altitude, with noticeable noise and a slow refresh.
source: Mass in the range of small-satellite GPS receivers (0.002 to 1.2 kg, for example a 0.16 kg unit); NASA State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology, chapter 5 (Guidance, Navigation and Control). Noise, update rate, dropout and cost are game values.

name: Precise altimeter
tradeoff: A steady, accurate altitude reading several times a second.
source: Mass at the top of the range of small-satellite GPS receivers (0.002 to 1.2 kg); NASA State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology, chapter 5 (Guidance, Navigation and Control). Noise, update rate, dropout and cost are game values.

name: Sun sensor
tradeoff: Tells roughly which way the craft points, to about a degree.
source: Coarse sun sensors: about 0.045 kg and 1 degree; NASA State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology, chapter 5 (Guidance, Navigation and Control). Noise, update rate, dropout and cost are game values.

name: Star tracker
tradeoff: Knows the craft's direction to a few arcseconds.
source: Star trackers: 0.04 to 3 kg, a few arcseconds (for example a 0.275 kg unit with 6 arcseconds); NASA State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology, chapter 5 (Guidance, Navigation and Control). Noise, update rate, dropout and cost are game values.

name: Fuel gauge
tradeoff: Shows the propellant left; without it you fly on your own arithmetic.
source: Estimate; not taken from a source. All values are game values.

name: Temperature sensor
tradeoff: Warns before the craft overheats.
source: Estimate; not taken from a source. All values are game values.

name: Basic proximity radar
tradeoff: Sees nearby objects late and only as blips.
source: Estimate. Range, mass, noise and cost are game values, scaled down from the top tier.

name: Tracking proximity radar
tradeoff: Gives the distance and bearing of objects in time to react.
source: Estimate. Range, mass, noise and cost are game values, scaled down from the top tier.

name: Long-range rendezvous radar
tradeoff: Sees shape and speed from far away, but is heavy and costly.
source: Range and mass modelled on the Apollo Lunar Module rendezvous radar: 400 nautical miles (740 km), about 80 lb (36 kg); NASA Apollo documents on the NASA Technical Reports Server. Noise, update rate and cost are game values.

name: Basic onboard computer
tradeoff: Runs the craft, but glitches when the Sun acts up.
source: Estimate in the range of small-satellite flight computers; NASA State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology, command and data handling chapter. All values are game values.

name: Radiation-hardened computer
tradeoff: Keeps every panel steady through a solar flare.
source: Estimate in the range of small-satellite flight computers; NASA State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology, command and data handling chapter. All values are game values.

name: Basic Earth camera
tradeoff: Light and cheap, with a modest data rate.
source: Estimate for an instrument of this class on a small satellite, not taken from one instrument; see NASA CubeSat 101 and the NASA State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology report for the class. All values are game values. The mission_fit ratings are game values.

name: High-resolution Earth camera
tradeoff: Sharp pictures and a lot of data, for more mass, power and money.
source: Estimate for an instrument of this class on a small satellite, not taken from one instrument; see NASA CubeSat 101 and the NASA State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology report for the class. All values are game values. The mission_fit ratings are game values.

name: Magnetometer
tradeoff: Measures the magnetic field for space-weather science; of no use for pictures.
source: Mass in the range of small-satellite magnetometers (0.006 to 0.33 kg); NASA State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology, chapter 5 (Guidance, Navigation and Control). Power, data rate, science value and cost are game values. The mission_fit ratings are game values.

name: Atmosphere probe
tradeoff: Samples the thin upper atmosphere; wants a low orbit.
source: Estimate for an instrument of this class on a small satellite, not taken from one instrument; see NASA CubeSat 101 and the NASA State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology report for the class. All values are game values. The mission_fit ratings are game values.

name: Imaging radar
tradeoff: Maps the surface through cloud and at night, but is the heaviest and hungriest instrument.
source: Estimate for an instrument of this class on a small satellite, not taken from one instrument; see NASA CubeSat 101 and the NASA State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology report for the class. All values are game values. The mission_fit ratings are game values.
